reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This paper describes an integrated device for on-chip generation of difference frequency mixing based on the use of thin film lithium niobate. The use of lithium niobate waveguides modified by poling for wavemixing processes is fairly widely used, including in commercially available devices. This approach, however, has modest efficiency and requires large pump power, resulting in [practical limitations. The work described in the manuscript overcomes this limitation and achieves unprecedented conversion efficiency of 31.7%. The approach is based on overcoming the major limitation of poling the waveguide with phase matching approaching the theoretical values. This is achieved by matching the poling to the unavoidable inhomogeneity of the waveguide thickness. The authors devised a metrology apparatus to measure the nm- scale thickness inhomogeneity and implement the poling period for optimized phase matching. As a result, their device can generate a maximum power output of12.26 dBm with normalized conversion efficiency exceeding 100% /(W cm^2).
This is a well-written paper that provides comprehensive technical details for the experimental measurements. It also demonstrates the ability to convert information outside the bandwidth of an EDFA (at1638 nm) to idler at 1556 nm, which falls within the EDFA bandwidth. This capability is useful for applications in PIC-based optical communication.
I recommend the paper for publication and urge the authors to clarify what are the sources of loss in their experimental setup and if they are accounted for in reporting their efficiency numbers.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors employ a recently invented technique, adapted poling, to maintain phase matching along the length of a PPLN waveguide for difference frequency generation (DFG). They demonstrate a real conversion efficiency of ~30 % and on-chip idler power nearly 20 mW, in addition to wide tunability.
The adapted poling method is new and powerful, only utilized in, to my knowledge, a few works to date. This, along with the significantly enhanced power/efficiency compared to other works, make the paper nearly worthy of publication in Nature Communications. Below, I raise some issues that I feel should be addressed before reconsidering the paper for publication.
My main concern is how the power and efficiency numbers are reported. Results which stress "record high" powers and/or efficiencies should be careful with the significant digits carried in various quantities and report errors/uncertainties. For instance, the authors claim a conversion efficiency of 31.75 %, but I am sure the uncertainty on this figure exceeds several percent, as there are numerous assumptions and sources of error. For instance, the chip coupling losses are assumed to be symmetric (in-coupling equals out-coupling), and the signal/idler losses are assumed equal.
How are the various optical powers measured? It seems implied that they are extracted from an optical spectrum analyzer (OSA). Is the setup calibrated for other losses between the chip and OSA? Is the OSA itself calibrated (they can be inaccurate)?
Given that the adapted poling method is central to the work, I feel the authors should provide more detail around its implementation. How does the poling period profile shown in Fig. 1(d) connect to the thickness various? There is a clear correlation, but no analysis is given. Were any different poling period profiles tried?
Why is Fig. 2(f) not closer to Fig. 2(d)? i.e., what are the limits of the adapted poling method? On a related note, I think Fig. 2(h) could be explained better. Will the normalized CE continue increasing with smaller step sizes? Is 200 um the smallest achievable step size?

Response: We sincerely thank Reviewer #1 for constructive suggestions and the positive assessment of our work. We appreciate the opportunity to provide a detailed response and revisions addressing the raised questions.
For a comprehensive evaluation of interacting wave power values, we conducted systematic experiments to characterize the insertion loss (IL) of components in the experimental setup and the coupling losses for pump, signal, and idler waves.
At the input side, we first measured the pump power output from the laser using a visible to near-infrared light photodetector based on silicon, obtaining a value of 26.7 dBm. Subsequent measurements revealed the following power reductions: 26.3 dBm after passing through a polarization controller (PC), 25.8 dBm after a wavelength division multiplexer (WDM), and 25.3 dBm after an additional WDM component, as illustrated in Fig. R1(a). Similarly, for the signal wave from the erbium-doped fiber amplifier (EDFA), we measured 29.0 dBm using a communication-band photodetector, which decreased to 28.5 dBm after a PC and further reduced to 27.5 dBm after passing through two WDMs. These measurements indicated that the IL of a PC and a WDM for the pump (signal) wave were 0.4 (0.5) dB and 0.5 (0.5) dB, respectively.
For waveguide-fiber coupling, we employed two lens fibers as shown in Fig. R1(b), achieving a maximum power of 12.3 dBm for the pump wave after careful calibration between the lens fibers and waveguides under the condition of turning on the pump light and turning off the signal light. The coupling loss for the signal wave was estimated under the condition that the pump wave has a minimum coupler loss, so we achieved a power of 13.8 dBm for the signal wave between the lens fibers and waveguides under the condition of turning on the signal light and turning off the pump light. Assuming symmetric coupling losses, we calculated the coupling loss as 6.5 dB/facet for the pump and 6.8 dB/facet for the signal. Consequently, the input pump and signal powers were determined to be 26.7 dBm – 0.4 dB – 0.5 dB – 6.5 dB= 19.3 dBm and 29.0 dBm – 0.5 dB – 0.5 dB – 6.8 dB = 21.2 dBm, respectively.
The revised on-chip pump power showed a slight decrease compared to previous results, primarily due to the inclusion of PC and WDM ILs, which accounted for an approximately 1 dB deviation in pump power evaluation. Additionally, the updated fiber-waveguide coupling loss was slightly lower than previously reported, as we implemented power calibration for the optical spectrum analyzer (OSA) to ensure consistency with photodetector measurements.
Through these refined measurements, we obtained updated on-chip power values of 13.2 dBm for the idler wave using the calibrated OSA. Based on these measurements, we calculated the difference frequency generation (DFG) conversion efficiency (CE) to be 48.6%. After addressing all potential error sources and accounting for component losses in the experimental setup, we conducted further experiments and updated the power and efficiency values in the manuscript accordingly.

Unlike couplers based on gratings or inverse taper structures, the edge couplers used here were based on broadened waveguides and had advantages in broadband coupling performances. The coupling efficiency mainly dominated by the modal overlap between the output light spot from lens fiber and the fundamental TE mode in waveguides. ### Reviewer 1

This paper describes an integrated device for on-chip generation of difference frequency mixing based on the use of thin film lithium niobate. The use of lithium niobate waveguides modified by poling for wavemixing processes is fairly widely used, including in commercially available devices. This approach, however, has modest efficiency and requires large pump power, resulting in [practical limitations. The work described in the manuscript overcomes this limitation and achieves unprecedented conversion efficiency of 31.7%. The approach is based on overcoming the major limitation of poling the waveguide with phase matching approaching the theoretical values. This is achieved by matching the poling to the unavoidable inhomogeneity of the waveguide thickness. The authors devised a metrology apparatus to measure the nm- scale thickness inhomogeneity and implement the poling period for optimized phase matching. As a result, their device can generate a maximum power output of12.26 dBm with normalized conversion efficiency exceeding 100% /(W cm^2).
This is a well-written paper that provides comprehensive technical details for the experimental measurements. It also demonstrates the ability to convert information outside the bandwidth of an EDFA (at1638 nm) to idler at 1556 nm, which falls within the EDFA bandwidth. This capability is useful for applications in PIC-based optical communication.
I recommend the paper for publication and urge the authors to clarify what are the sources of loss in their experimental setup and if they are accounted for in reporting their efficiency numbers.

### Reviewer 2

The authors employ a recently invented technique, adapted poling, to maintain phase matching along the length of a PPLN waveguide for difference frequency generation (DFG). They demonstrate a real conversion efficiency of ~30 % and on-chip idler power nearly 20 mW, in addition to wide tunability.
The adapted poling method is new and powerful, only utilized in, to my knowledge, a few works to date. This, along with the significantly enhanced power/efficiency compared to other works, make the paper nearly worthy of publication in Nature Communications. Below, I raise some issues that I feel should be addressed before reconsidering the paper for publication.
My main concern is how the power and efficiency numbers are reported. Results which stress "record high" powers and/or efficiencies should be careful with the significant digits carried in various quantities and report errors/uncertainties. For instance, the authors claim a conversion efficiency of 31.75 %, but I am sure the uncertainty on this figure exceeds several percent, as there are numerous assumptions and sources of error. For instance, the chip coupling losses are assumed to be symmetric (in-coupling equals out-coupling), and the signal/idler losses are assumed equal.
How are the various optical powers measured? It seems implied that they are extracted from an optical spectrum analyzer (OSA). Is the setup calibrated for other losses between the chip and OSA? Is the OSA itself calibrated (they can be inaccurate)?
Given that the adapted poling method is central to the work, I feel the authors should provide more detail around its implementation. How does the poling period profile shown in Fig. 1(d) connect to the thickness various? There is a clear correlation, but no analysis is given. Were any different poling period profiles tried?
Why is Fig. 2(f) not closer to Fig. 2(d)? i.e., what are the limits of the adapted poling method? On a related note, I think Fig. 2(h) could be explained better. Will the normalized CE continue increasing with smaller step sizes? Is 200 um the smallest achievable step size?

For a comprehensive evaluation of interacting wave power values, we conducted systematic experiments to characterize the insertion loss (IL) of components in the experimental setup and the coupling losses for pump, signal, and idler waves.
At the input side, we first measured the pump power output from the laser using a visible to near-infrared light photodetector based on silicon, obtaining a value of 26.7 dBm. Subsequent measurements revealed the following power reductions: 26.3 dBm after passing through a polarization controller (PC), 25.8 dBm after a wavelength division multiplexer (WDM), and 25.3 dBm after an additional WDM component, as illustrated in Fig. R1(a). Similarly, for the signal wave from the erbium-doped fiber amplifier (EDFA), we measured 29.0 dBm using a communication-band photodetector, which decreased to 28.5 dBm after a PC and further reduced to 27.5 dBm after passing through two WDMs. These measurements indicated that the IL of a PC and a WDM for the pump (signal) wave were 0.4 (0.5) dB and 0.5 (0.5) dB, respectively.
For waveguide-fiber coupling, we employed two lens fibers as shown in Fig. R1(b), achieving a maximum power of 12.3 dBm for the pump wave after careful calibration between the lens fibers and waveguides under the condition of turning on the pump light and turning off the signal light. The coupling loss for the signal wave was estimated under the condition that the pump wave has a minimum coupler loss, so we achieved a power of 13.8 dBm for the signal wave between the lens fibers and waveguides under the condition of turning on the signal light and turning off the pump light. Assuming symmetric coupling losses, we calculated the coupling loss as 6.5 dB/facet for the pump and 6.8 dB/facet for the signal. Consequently, the input pump and signal powers were determined to be 26.7 dBm – 0.4 dB – 0.5 dB – 6.5 dB= 19.3 dBm and 29.0 dBm – 0.5 dB – 0.5 dB – 6.8 dB = 21.2 dBm, respectively.
The revised on-chip pump power showed a slight decrease compared to previous results, primarily due to the inclusion of PC and WDM ILs, which accounted for an approximately 1 dB deviation in pump power evaluation. Additionally, the updated fiber-waveguide coupling loss was slightly lower than previously reported, as we implemented power calibration for the optical spectrum analyzer (OSA) to ensure consistency with photodetector measurements.
Through these refined measurements, we obtained updated on-chip power values of 13.2 dBm for the idler wave using the calibrated OSA. Based on these measurements, we calculated the difference frequency generation (DFG) conversion efficiency (CE) to be 48.6%. After addressing all potential error sources and accounting for component losses in the experimental setup, we conducted further experiments and updated the power and efficiency values in the manuscript accordingly.

The quasi-phase matching requirement along the waveguide can be expressed as
n_eff,p(lambda_p, t) - n_eff,s(lambda_s, t) - n_eff,i(lambda_i, t) = m * lambda_p / Lambda(t)
where m = ±1, ±2, ±3…is the index of phase-matching order. Considering the first order of the phase-matching condition, the poling period distributions along the periodically-poled TFLN waveguide can be expressed as:
Lambda(t) = lambda_p / (n_eff,p(lambda_p, t) - n_eff,s(lambda_s, t) - n_eff,i(lambda_i, t))

In adapted-poling implementations, the conversion efficiency limit mainly originates from the thickness measuring resolution along the waveguide, due to the uncertainty in the exact waveguide thickness between the adjacent measured points. This can result in phase mismatches in practical adapted-poling devices, ultimately disrupting the DFG process. Therefore, smaller measurement step sizes will have higher conversion efficiency. In our experimental setup, the smallest achievable step size is limited to 200 μm since the light spot from the measuring instrument exposed on the chip surface has a diameter of around 100~200 μm. As a result, the measured thickness represents thickness information over a 200×200 μm2 area. Nevertheless, further reduction of the step size cannot significantly improve conversion efficiency because the already achieved efficiency remains relatively high.

### Reviewer 1

This paper describes an integrated device for on-chip generation of difference frequency mixing based on the use of thin film lithium niobate. The use of lithium niobate waveguides modified by poling for wavemixing processes is fairly widely used, including in commercially available devices. This approach, however, has modest efficiency and requires large pump power, resulting in [practical limitations. The work described in the manuscript overcomes this limitation and achieves unprecedented conversion efficiency of 31.7%. The approach is based on overcoming the major limitation of poling the waveguide with phase matching approaching the theoretical values. This is achieved by matching the poling to the unavoidable inhomogeneity of the waveguide thickness. The authors devised a metrology apparatus to measure the nm- scale thickness inhomogeneity and implement the poling period for optimized phase matching. As a result, their device can generate a maximum power output of12.26 dBm with normalized conversion efficiency exceeding 100% /(W cm^2).
This is a well-written paper that provides comprehensive technical details for the experimental measurements. It also demonstrates the ability to convert information outside the bandwidth of an EDFA (at1638 nm) to idler at 1556 nm, which falls within the EDFA bandwidth. This capability is useful for applications in PIC-based optical communication.
I recommend the paper for publication and urge the authors to clarify what are the sources of loss in their experimental setup and if they are accounted for in reporting their efficiency numbers.

### Reviewer 2

The authors employ a recently invented technique, adapted poling, to maintain phase matching along the length of a PPLN waveguide for difference frequency generation (DFG). They demonstrate a real conversion efficiency of ~30 % and on-chip idler power nearly 20 mW, in addition to wide tunability.
The adapted poling method is new and powerful, only utilized in, to my knowledge, a few works to date. This, along with the significantly enhanced power/efficiency compared to other works, make the paper nearly worthy of publication in Nature Communications. Below, I raise some issues that I feel should be addressed before reconsidering the paper for publication.
My main concern is how the power and efficiency numbers are reported. Results which stress "record high" powers and/or efficiencies should be careful with the significant digits carried in various quantities and report errors/uncertainties. For instance, the authors claim a conversion efficiency of 31.75 %, but I am sure the uncertainty on this figure exceeds several percent, as there are numerous assumptions and sources of error. For instance, the chip coupling losses are assumed to be symmetric (in-coupling equals out-coupling), and the signal/idler losses are assumed equal.
How are the various optical powers measured? It seems implied that they are extracted from an optical spectrum analyzer (OSA). Is the setup calibrated for other losses between the chip and OSA? Is the OSA itself calibrated (they can be inaccurate)?
Given that the adapted poling method is central to the work, I feel the authors should provide more detail around its implementation. How does the poling period profile shown in Fig. 1(d) connect to the thickness various? There is a clear correlation, but no analysis is given. Were any different poling period profiles tried?

Response: We sincerely thank Reviewer #1 for constructive suggestions and the positive assessment of our work. We appreciate the opportunity to provide a detailed response and revisions addressing the raised questions.
For a comprehensive evaluation of interacting wave power values, we conducted systematic experiments to characterize the insertion loss (IL) of components in the experimental setup and the coupling losses for pump, signal, and idler waves.
At the input side, we first measured the pump power output from the laser using a visible to near-infrared light photodetector based on silicon, obtaining a value of 26.7 dBm. Subsequent measurements revealed the following power reductions: 26.3 dBm after passing through a polarization controller (PC), 25.8 dBm after a wavelength division multiplexer (WDM), and 25.3 dBm after an additional WDM component, as illustrated in Fig. R1(a). Similarly, for the signal wave from the erbium-doped fiber amplifier (EDFA), we measured 29.0 dBm using a communication-band photodetector, which decreased to 28.5 dBm after a PC and further reduced to 27.5 dBm after passing through two WDMs. These measurements indicated that the IL of a PC and a WDM for the pump (signal) wave were 0.4 (0.5) dB and 0.5 (0.5) dB, respectively.
For waveguide-fiber coupling, we employed two lens fibers as shown in Fig. R1(b), achieving a maximum power of 12.3 dBm for the pump wave after careful calibration between the lens fibers and waveguides under the condition of turning on the pump light and turning off the signal light. The coupling loss for the signal wave was estimated under the condition that the pump wave has a minimum coupler loss, so we achieved a power of 13.8 dBm for the signal wave between the lens fibers and waveguides under the condition of turning on the signal light and turning off the pump light. Assuming symmetric coupling losses, we calculated the coupling loss as 6.5 dB/facet for the pump and 6.8 dB/facet for the signal. Consequently, the input pump and signal powers were determined to be 26.7 dBm – 0.4 dB – 0.5 dB – 6.5 dB= 19.3 dBm and 29.0 dBm – 0.5 dB – 0.5 dB – 6.8 dB = 21.2 dBm, respectively.

General comment: The authors employ a recently invented technique, adapted poling, to maintain phase matching along the length of a PPLN waveguide for difference frequency generation (DFG). They demonstrate a real conversion efficiency of ~30 % and on-chip idler power nearly 20 mW, in addition to wide tunability.
The adapted poling method is new and powerful, only utilized in, to my knowledge, a few works to date. This, along with the significantly enhanced power/efficiency compared to other works, make the paper nearly worthy of publication in Nature Communications. Below, I raise some issues that I feel should be addressed before reconsidering the paper for publication.
Response: We sincerely thank Reviewer #2 for constructive suggestions and the positive assessment of our work. We appreciate the opportunity to provide a detailed response and revisions addressing the raised questions. First, we implemented a comprehensive recalibration of the optical spectrum analyzer (OSA) to ensure precise alignment between its power measurements and those obtained from the photodetector. This recalibration process led us to re-evaluate the insertion losses (IL) associated with the polarization controller (PC), wavelength division multiplexer (WDM), and coupling losses for the interacting waves as well as accurately recharacterize the on-chip powers, absolute efficiencies, and normalized efficiencies of wavelength conversion. Second, we have expanded the discussion of our poling implementation in the supplementary materials, including a detailed mathematical expression for poling period calculation. Furthermore, we have provided a thorough explanation of the technical constraints that establish 200 μm as the minimum achievable step size in our experimental setup. In the following sections, we address each of the reviewer’s comments individually.
Comment 1: My main concern is how the power and efficiency numbers are reported. Results which stress "record high" powers and/or efficiencies should be careful with the significant digits carried in various quantities and report errors/uncertainties. For instance, the authors claim a conversion efficiency of 31.75 %, but I am sure the uncertainty on this figure exceeds several percent, as there are numerous assumptions and sources of error. For instance, the chip coupling losses are assumed to be symmetric (in-coupling equals out-coupling), and the signal/idler losses are assumed equal. How are the various optical powers measured? It seems implied that they are extracted from an optical spectrum analyzer (OSA). Is the setup calibrated for other losses between the chip and OSA? Is the OSA itself calibrated (they can be inaccurate)?
Response: Thank you for the comment. For coupling loss symmetry, the chip facets used edge couplers that had identical designing and processing procedures. Besides, lens fibers of same type were used to couple light between fibers and waveguides on-chip. So, it is reasonable to assume that the chip coupling losses are symmetric. Unlike couplers based on gratings or inverse taper structures, the edge couplers used here were based on broadened waveguides and had advantages in broadband coupling performances. The coupling efficiency mainly dominated by the modal overlap between the output light spot from lens fiber and the fundamental TE mode in waveguides. And the modal profiles between signal and idler wave are quite similar because their wavelengths are so close, as shown in Fig. R2. At the edge coupler, the effective modal field areas for signal (1608 nm) and idler (1584 nm) wave were calculated as 2.082 μm2 and 2.063 μm2, respectively. The slight difference (<1%) in modal field area ensures the similar coupling losses for signal and idler wave.
Figure R2. Simulated modal profiles of signal (left) and idler (right) at edge couplers.
For a comprehensive evaluation of interacting wave power values, we conducted systematic experiments to characterize the insertion loss (IL) of components in the experimental setup and the coupling losses for pump, signal, and idler waves.
At the input side, we first measured the pump power output from the laser using a visible to near-infrared light photodetector based on silicon, obtaining a value of 26.7 dBm. Subsequent measurements revealed the following power reductions: 26.3 dBm after passing through a polarization controller (PC), 25.8 dBm after a wavelength division multiplexer (WDM), and 25.3 dBm after an additional WDM component, as illustrated in Fig. R3(a). Similarly, for the signal wave from the erbium-doped fiber amplifier (EDFA), we measured 29.0 dBm using a communication-band photodetector, which decreased to 28.5 dBm after a PC and further reduced to 27.5 dBm after passing through two WDMs. These measurements indicated that the IL of a PC and a WDM for the pump (signal) wave were 0.4 (0.5) dB and 0.5 (0.5) dB, respectively.
For waveguide-fiber coupling, we employed two lens fibers as shown in Fig. R3(b), achieving a maximum power of 12.3 dBm for the pump wave after careful calibration between the lens fibers and waveguides under the condition of turning on the pump light and turning off the signal light. The coupling loss for the signal wave was estimated under the condition that the pump wave has a minimum coupler loss, so we achieved a power of 13.8 dBm for the signal wave between the lens fibers and waveguides under the condition of turning on the signal light and turning off the pump light. Assuming symmetric coupling losses, we calculated the coupling loss as 6.5 dB/facet for the pump and 6.8 dB/facet for the signal. Consequently, the input pump and signal powers were determined to be 26.7 dBm – 0.4 dB – 0.5 dB – 6.5 dB= 19.3 dBm and 29.0 dBm – 0.5 dB – 0.5 dB – 6.8 dB = 21.2 dBm, respectively.
The revised on-chip pump power showed a slight decrease compared to previous results, primarily due to the inclusion of PC and WDM ILs, which accounted for an approximately 1 dB deviation in pump power evaluation. Additionally, the updated fiber-waveguide coupling loss was slightly lower than previously reported, as we implemented power calibration for the optical spectrum analyzer (OSA) to ensure consistency with photodetector measurements.
Through these refined measurements, we obtained updated on-chip power values of 13.2 dBm for the idler wave using the calibrated OSA. Based on these measurements, we calculated the difference frequency generation (DFG) conversion efficiency (CE) to be 48.6%. After addressing all potential error sources and accounting for component losses in the experimental setup, we conducted further experiments and updated the power and efficiency values in the manuscript accordingly.

Response: Thank you for your comment. We have added some details around adapted poling implementation in the supplementary material. At first, the effective refractive indices of the pump (n ), signal (n ), and idler (n ) waves as a function of film thickness t are plotted in Figs. R4(a)-(c), which can be expressed as n = 1.987+0.0001795t, n = 1.671+0.0004048t, and n = 1.680+0.0003996t when the film thickness variation is less than 20 nm.
Fig. R4. (a) Calculated effective refractive index of pump (a), signal (b), and idler (c) waves under different TFLN layer thickness.
The quasi-phase matching requirement along the waveguide can be expressed as
n_eff,p(lambda_p, t) - n_eff,s(lambda_s, t) - n_eff,i(lambda_i, t) = m * lambda_p / Lambda(t)
where m = ±1, ±2, ±3…is the index of phase-matching order. Considering the first order of the phase-matching condition, the poling period distributions along the periodically-poled TFLN waveguide can be expressed as:
Lambda(t) = lambda_p / (n_eff,p(lambda_p, t) - n_eff,s(lambda_s, t) - n_eff,i(lambda_i, t))
Therefore, the relationship between poling period and film thickness can be expressed as shown in Fig. R5(a).
Fig. R5. (a) Calculated poling period of DFG with different TFLN layer thickness. (b) Simulated effective propagation constant mismatch with different TFLN layer thickness.
As for different poling period profiles, we have so far only tried a measurement step size of 200 μm. In adapted-poling implementations, the conversion efficiency limit mainly originates from the thickness measuring resolution along the waveguide, due to the uncertainty in the exact waveguide thickness between the adjacent measured points. This can result in phase mismatches in practical adapted-poling devices, ultimately disrupting the DFG process. Therefore, smaller measurement step sizes will have higher conversion efficiency. In our experimental setup, the smallest achievable step size is limited to 200 μm since the light spot from the measuring instrument exposed on the chip surface has a diameter of around 100~200 μm. As a result, the measured thickness represents thickness information over a 200×200 μm2 area. Nevertheless, further reduction of the step size cannot significantly improve conversion efficiency because the already achieved efficiency remains relatively high.
